column1: Which preterites change stem in the third person only, and how?
column2:
-ir stem-changers, in él and ellos:
pedir → pidió, pidieron · dormir → durmió, durmieron

-ar and -er verbs do not stem-change in the preterite: volver → volví.

column1:
When and why do you use the
Pretérito perfecto simple?
column2:
A completed event, viewed as a whole. Something happened, and the sentence treats it as finished. This is the tense that moves a story forward.
  • A single finished action — ayer comí paella.
  • A sequence of events — entré, me senté y pedí un café.
  • Stated duration or repetition count — viví allí tres años; lo llamé cinco veces. A bounded span is still bounded.
  • Start or end of something — empezó a llover.
Not about how long, but about whether the event is presented as a completed whole. Contrast with the imperfect: preterite = photograph, imperfect = film running.

column1:
Tricks and tips for the
Pretérito perfecto simple
column2:
• -er and -ir are completely identical in this tense.
  • Accents carry the meaning: hablo (I speak) vs habló (he spoke); hable (subj.) vs hablé (I spoke).
  • Strong preterites take no accents: tuve, tuvo — never tuvé, tuvó. Reliable giveaway.
  • -j- stems drop the i: dijeron, trajeron, condujeron — not dijieron.
  • hablamos / vivimos are ambiguous with the present; comimos is not.
  • Learn the strong stems as a block — they recur unchanged in the imperfect subjunctive. One memorisation, two tenses.
